lead: Generative models learn from data people wrote or labelled. That data carries history: skewed samples, harsh language, few faces of some groups. A model can repeat and scale those patterns in text, images, voice and video. This chapter treats evaluation and mitigation as part of the model, not an afterthought: measure per-group errors, filter toxic output, mark synthetic media, protect private data and document limits. It is used in chatbots, image tools and media checks.
prereq: You need: 6.4 GANs and 6.6 applications; for text models, Unit 5 on large language models.

sections.h3: Bias is a measurable error pattern

blocks.text: Bias in a generative model is a group-dependent error or stereotype. It enters through training data and through the objective. If a group is rare in the data, the model sees fewer examples and may learn a coarse or wrong pattern. If the objective rewards average accuracy, the model can ignore the small group and still score well. A face generator trained mostly on one skin tone may distort others; a text model trained on skewed web text may link a profession to one gender.

Measure bias per group. For a classifier, report accuracy, false positive rate and false negative rate for each group. FPR = FP ÷ (FP + TN): the share of truly negative cases wrongly flagged. FNR = FN ÷ (FN + TP): the share of truly positive cases missed. These numbers expose harm that one overall score hides.

blocks.where: s_g is the share of group g that receives a positive decision; k is the number of groups; DPD is the demographic parity difference. DPD = 0 means equal selection rates, not equal error rates.

blocks.text: Mitigation starts before release: rebalance or reweight data, test per group, choose thresholds with the harm in mind, and document trade-offs. Fairness definitions conflict. Equal selection rates can coexist with unequal false positive rates. The team must state which definition it targets and why. Audits repeat these tests on fresh data.

Toxicity is harmful content: insults, threats, hate, harassment. A generative text model can produce it when a prompt pushes it. Red-teaming is adversarial testing: people try prompts, typos and role-play to break the model. Findings feed filters, refusal rules, training data cleanup and human review. Filters act on input and output, but they make false positives; context matters, and a blocked medical term is not the same as a slur.

A deepfake is synthetic image, voice or video made to look real. GANs and diffusion models make faces; voice cloning copies speech; video models animate a still face. Harms include fraud, non-consensual intimate images and political deception. Consent is central: a person's face or voice should not be used without permission. Provenance records where media came from; a watermark embeds a signal in the output. Detection uses classifiers trained to spot artefacts, but it is an arms race and never perfect.

Controls combine law, platform policy and technical checks. Technical checks include watermark detection, provenance metadata and human verification for high-stakes claims. A detector gives evidence, not proof. The worked example shows how to score one.

Generative models can memorize training data. A text model may repeat a phone number or a private message; an image model may copy a face. Mitigation: remove personal data, deduplicate, limit epochs, and use differential privacy, which adds noise so one record changes the output little. Test with extraction prompts that ask the model to repeat rare strings.

A model card is a short document released with a model. It states intended use, out-of-scope use, training data summary, evaluation metrics including per-group results, limitations and ethical risks. An audit is an independent test of those claims: bias probes, toxicity red-teaming, privacy extraction and deepfake checks. Documentation does not fix a model, but it makes harm visible and gives users a basis to choose.

Responsible AI is the process that ties these pieces together: define harms, measure them, mitigate, document and monitor after release. Some syllabi call this responsible AI; text-model courses may place it under LLM ethics, see Unit 5. The key exam point: evaluation and mitigation are part of the model, not an optional appendix.

figure.caption: The worked example as a confusion matrix: the left column holds videos the detector flagged as fake, the right column those it passed as real. The two highlighted cells are the errors — 50 real videos wrongly flagged (FPR = 50 ÷ 1,000 = 5%) and 100 fakes missed (FNR = 100 ÷ 1,000 = 10%), which leave precision at 900 ÷ 950 = 94.7%.

spec.title: Deepfake detector: 2,000 videos
spec.aria: A two-row confusion matrix for a deepfake detector on 1,000 real and 1,000 fake videos: 50 real videos flagged (FP), 950 real cleared (TN), 900 fakes caught (TP), 100 fakes missed (FN).

examples.question: A deepfake detector tests 1,000 real and 1,000 fake videos. It flags 50 real videos as fake and misses 100 fake videos. Compute false positive rate, false negative rate and precision.
steps: Real videos = 1,000. False positives FP = 50. True negatives TN = 1,000 − 50 = 950. FPR = 50 ÷ (50 + 950) = 50 ÷ 1,000 = 0.05 = 5%.
Fake videos = 1,000. False negatives FN = 100. True positives TP = 1,000 − 100 = 900. FNR = 100 ÷ (100 + 900) = 100 ÷ 1,000 = 0.10 = 10%.
Flagged videos = FP + TP = 50 + 900 = 950. Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP) = 900 ÷ 950 = 0.94737 ≈ 94.7%.
examples.check:
fp = 50
tn = 1000 - fp
fpr = fp / (fp + tn) * 100
fn = 100
tp = 1000 - fn
fnr = fn / (fn + tp) * 100
flagged = fp + tp
precision = tp / flagged * 100
print(f"{fpr:.1f}")
print(f"{fnr:.1f}")
print(f"{precision:.1f}")

traps: High overall accuracy hides harm when one group is small; report per-group false positive and false negative rates.
False positive rate is FP ÷ (FP + TN), not FP ÷ (FP + TP); precision is TP ÷ (TP + FP).
Demographic parity means equal selection rates, not equal error rates; a model can satisfy parity and still have unequal FPR.
A detector's precision depends on the base rate; 99% accuracy can mean low precision when fakes are rare.
A watermark proves origin only if it is present and intact; it is not detection of every fake.

quiz.a: It is the maximum selection rate across groups minus the minimum selection rate. Zero means equal selection rates.

quiz.q: Why can overall accuracy hide bias?
quiz.a: A small group contributes few errors, so the majority group dominates the average. Per-group FPR and FNR show the hidden harm.

quiz.q: Group A has 200 people: 10 false positives and 190 true negatives. Group B has 50 people: 5 false positives and 45 true negatives. Compute each FPR and the difference in percentage points.
quiz.a: Group A FPR = 10 ÷ (10 + 190) = 5%. Group B FPR = 5 ÷ (5 + 45) = 10%. Difference = 10% − 5% = 5 percentage points.

quiz.q: A deepfake detector has 99% accuracy. Fakes are 1% of videos. It catches 90% of fakes and flags 1% of real videos. Explain why precision is low and compute it roughly.
quiz.a: In 10,000 videos: 100 fake, 9,900 real. TP = 90. FP = 99. Precision = 90 ÷ (90 + 99) = 47.6%. Many real videos create false positives when fakes are rare.
Adversarial testing where people try prompts and inputs to make the model fail or produce harmful output; findings feed filters and training fixes.

quiz.q: Name three items in a model card.
quiz.a: Intended use, training data summary, evaluation metrics including per-group results, limitations, ethical risks.

quiz.q: Why is a watermark not a complete deepfake defence?
quiz.a: It may be removed or absent in unmarked generators. Detection, provenance, consent and human checks are also needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, teams use model cards, data statements and audits before release. Deepfake defence combines provenance signals, detection models and platform policy. Regulators are moving toward transparency duties for synthetic media. Search next for model cards, content provenance, red teaming, differential privacy and fairness metrics such as equalized odds.
